newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain allays British concerns over Gibraltar.
newsitem.headline: Spain allays British concerns over Gibraltar.

text.p: Spain assured Britain on Wednesday it would not impede the movement of Gibraltar residents through European Union territory, easing tensions between the two countries over the disputed colony.
Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes gave the assurance to his British opposite number Malcolm Rifkind at a joint news conference after the two discussed problems over Gibraltar.

"I would like to reaffirm that Spain recognises the right of Gibraltarians to freely circulate within EU territory and shall always act with respect to this right in accordance with EU law as it has always done," Matutes said.
Rifkind said Matutes had allayed concerns over the possibility that Spain would refuse to recognise British-issued passports for Gibraltar.
"I of course very much welcome that clarification and it will remove the anxiety that has been felt in the last weeks," Rifkind said.

Any problems with regard to passports were purely technical, not political, Matutes said. He did not elaborate further. Rifkind said only that the problems related to certain kinds of British passports used by some Gibraltar residents.

Spain reiterated its claim to sovereignty over Gibraltar, which lies at the tip of the Iberian peninsula and dominates the western entrance to the Mediterranean. But Matutes acknowledged it would take a "long time" to resolve this claim.
Any change of sovereignty must be based on consulting the people of Gibraltar, Rifkind said.

The two also discussed Spain's insistence on tougher measures to combat money-laundering and drug-trafficking which had been rife in Gibraltar. Matutes praised strong measures adopted by the British government but indicated that more needed to be done.
Matutes said Rifkind and the government of Gibraltar wanted to end Gibraltar's "opaque" financial system and adopt a transparent one which complies with all EU legislation.
Matutes also demanded that Spain be permitted to use Gibraltar's airport, which he said was agreed in a 1987 treaty. Local authorities have blocked Spain from using it, he said.

Rifkind responded that the issue involved difficult questions over sovereignty but added that he saw practical ways for people on both sides of the border to benefit from the airport. He expressed doubts, however, that any major progress would be achieved on Spain's demand in the short term.

Spain and Britain meet annually to discuss Gibraltar disputes. Gibraltar's new first minister, Peter Caruana, stayed away from the talks, the first since his election, despite a pledge to improve strained ties with both Britain and Spain.
Spain insisted that Gibraltar could only participate as part of the British delegation.
"We cannot have a third flag, a third party, a third voice," said Matutes.
